h1:
Pai Walking Street at Night
Street Food · Snacks · Sweets
intro: As the sun softens, Pai Walking Street in the town center (Chaisongkhram–Rangsiyanon Road) slowly wakes up. Cart vendors raise their umbrellas, light their burners and set up their woks, and the cool valley breeze rolls in carrying the smell of grilling meat, frying roti, and live music. This is the kind of dinner a lot of people come to Pai specifically to walk and graze through — strolling slowly, tasting one bite at a time, paying 10–20 THB a go, and ending up comfortably full by the end of the street. We've pulled together what's worth trying, the stalls people talk about, and the timing that makes the walk most fun.

blocks.html: Pai Walking Street is open every day, no days off. Stalls start setting up around 5pm, are mostly in full swing by 6pm, and peak between 7–9pm before they begin packing up around 10–11pm. The street runs roughly 500–1,000 meters depending on the high or low season, and it's an easy 30-minute stroll end to end. Both sides are lined with savory food, sweets, drinks, handmade goods, clothes and souvenirs, broken up here and there by sit-down spots and live-music bars.

blocks.title: Read before you go
blocks.html: Bring plenty of small bills and coins. Almost every cart takes cash only, and a lot of items go for 10 THB, so having 10-baht coins on hand makes grazing much smoother. In high season (Nov–Feb) it gets crowded and the air turns cool, so pack a light jacket too.

blocks.text: Savory bites to graze one at a time

blocks.html: The charm of this street is "small portions, small prices" — it's built for sampling several stalls in a single meal, so you don't have to order a big plate and fill up at the first one. We've ordered these by what people mention most often and what you can find easily all the way down the street.

items.name: Miang Kham in wild betel leaf (Pai Minis, riverside)
items.blurb: One bite, every flavor at once — ginger, lime, chili, shallot, toasted coconut and peanuts wrapped in a wild betel leaf and drizzled with miang sauce. It's the signature of a tiny riverside stall that sells them at 10 THB a piece, a great easy way to kick off your grazing.

items.name: Khao soi (chicken) — stall near 7-Eleven
items.blurb: Egg noodles in a northern-style coconut curry broth, topped with crispy fried noodles, served with chicken or beef and eaten alongside pickled greens and shallots. It's the northern Thai dish you can find on this street, and the stall near the 7-Eleven is a spot people stop at often.

items.name: Grilled pork, sausage & meatball skewers
items.blurb: Rows of skewers grilling the whole length of the street — pork, chicken, sausage, meatballs, and at some stalls oddities like offal if you want to try them. It's the easiest walk-and-eat food to carry along. Near Hey Mom café at the end of the street there are skewers for 5 THB each too.

items.name: Gyoza & dim sum (steamed or fried)
items.blurb: Gyoza and dim sum stalls with fillings to choose from — shrimp, squid, vegetable, chicken, pork — both steamed hot and fried crispy, dipped in sauce and eaten bite by bite as you walk. Just right between stalls.

items.name: Pad thai cooked fresh in the wok
items.blurb: Stir-fried fresh in a hot wok right in front of you, available as a regular plate or as a "mini pad thai" at Pai Minis for 10 THB a portion so you can try it without filling up on a whole plate.

items.name: Spring rolls (near the pink ATM)
items.blurb: A spring-roll stall with several fillings, including mushroom and corn, available either fried crispy or fresh, with spicy and sweet-and-sour dipping sauces. Easy to spot — it's right by the pink ATM.

items.name: Sakoo sai moo (pork-filled tapioca dumplings)
items.blurb: A soft, chewy snack with a savory pork filling. Some stalls serve it with slices of papaya to cut the richness. A 10-baht bite that's good for lining your stomach as you walk.

items.name: Grilled & boiled corn
items.blurb: A classic walk-and-eat that Pai's cool air makes taste even better — grilled and brushed with butter, or boiled sweet, warm in your hand as you stroll.

items.name: Som tam & fried snacks
items.blurb: Fresh papaya-salad and fried-snack stalls are scattered down the street — som tam thai, som tam with crab and fermented fish, paired with fried chicken or hot fried bites — for anyone who wants a punch of bold, spicy flavor between the sweets.

blocks.title: How to graze and get your money's worth
blocks.html: Don't fill up at the first stall. Start with small bites like miang kham, spring rolls and skewers, then close with a main like khao soi or pad thai if you still have room. This way you get to try several vendors in one meal without wasting stomach space.

blocks.text: Sweets & drinks to finish on a cool note

blocks.html: Once you've grazed enough savory food, the dessert side is the highlight a lot of people wait for — from cooling treats to beat the heat to warm, fragrant sweets that go perfectly with Pai's cool air.

items.name: Coconut ice cream in a whole coconut
items.blurb: Coconut ice cream served in a real coconut shell, topped with peanuts, sweet corn and sticky rice. It's an easy-to-find cool dessert that photographs well, sold all along the street.

items.name: Banana–Nutella roti
items.blurb: Thin dough fried on a hot griddle, filled with banana, condensed milk or Nutella, cut into pieces and dusted with sugar. You can smell it before you reach the stall — a warm dessert that pairs beautifully with the cool breeze.

items.name: Mini coconut pancakes (kanom krok style)
items.blurb: At Pai Minis you'll find bite-sized coconut pancakes — 6 pieces served hot for 10 THB, fragrant with coconut milk, crisp outside and soft inside. A small-bite sweet that's easy to keep nibbling.

items.name: Mango sticky rice
items.blurb: Coconut-soaked sticky rice with slices of ripe mango — the Thai dessert international visitors line up for during mango season.

items.name: Grilled black sticky rice / black sticky rice pancake
items.blurb: Black sticky rice drizzled with condensed milk and palm sugar — warm, sweet and rich. It's a local treat you can find on this street and one that suits the cold weather.

items.name: Refillable milk tea in a "bamboo cup"
items.blurb: Milk tea / bubble tea in the bamboo cups Pai is known for. Buy the first cup for around 40 THB, then take the cup to a refill point and top up for 10 THB each — it's both a drink and a souvenir to carry as you walk.

items.name: Thai tea, fresh coconut & fruit smoothies
items.blurb: Sweet, creamy iced Thai tea, fresh fragrant coconut water, or blended fruit smoothies — easy on the wallet and cooling as you walk, good to carry alongside your walk-and-eat snacks.

blocks.title: Local Tai Yai dishes
blocks.html: Pai sits in Mae Hong Son, which has a Tai Yai (Shan)–Yunnan culture. If you want to try genuinely local flavors for a meal, it's worth heading to the morning market or to restaurants in town (see the Mae Hong Son food guide linked below). The Walking Street itself leans mainly toward walk-and-eat street food and sweets.

blocks.text: What time to go, where to park, how to walk it

items: Best time — 6:30–8pm, when all the stalls are open but the crowd isn't too thick yet. If you come from 9pm onward, some stalls have sold out or started packing up.

Getting there — Pai town is small, so it's an easy walk from any in-town accommodation to the Walking Street. If you drive or ride a motorbike, find parking on the outskirts and walk in, since the road closes to become a pedestrian street in the evening.
Budget per person — grazing on 5–6 small bites runs about 100–200 THB and fills you up; add a main dish and a dessert and it's around 200–300 THB.
Cash — bring small bills and 10-baht coins. Most stalls don't take transfers or cards, and the line moves much faster when you have exact change.
Etiquette — the street is narrow and busy, so keep to the right, don't stand blocking a stall front, and put your trash in the bins. It helps keep this little town pleasant to walk through.

faq.q: What days and hours is Pai Walking Street open?
faq.a: It's open every day with no days off. Stalls start setting up around 5pm, are mostly open by 6pm, peak between 7–9pm, then pack up around 10–11pm. The most fun window to walk is 6:30–8pm.

faq.q: How much do you need to spend to get full at Pai Walking Street?
faq.a: If you graze on 5–6 small bites priced at 10–30 THB, it runs about 100–200 THB per person and fills you up. Add a main like khao soi or pad thai plus a dessert and it's around 200–300 THB.

faq.q: What 10-baht foods are there in Pai?
faq.a: Plenty — miang kham, mini pad thai, spring rolls, pork-filled tapioca dumplings, grilled corn, mini coconut pancakes, and black sticky rice with condensed milk. Some stalls at the end of the street have 5-baht skewers too.

faq.q: What are the best desserts to try at Pai Walking Street?
faq.a: Coconut ice cream in a coconut shell, banana–Nutella roti, mini coconut pancakes, and mango sticky rice. As for drinks, the popular one is the bamboo-cup milk tea where you buy the first cup and refill for 10 THB each.

faq.q: Do I need to bring cash to Pai Walking Street?
faq.a: Yes, plan on cash. Almost all the carts take cash and many items cost 10 THB, so keeping small bills and 10-baht coins on hand makes grazing and paying much smoother.
